label: Lost the fight
title: The Queen of Hawaii vs. the United States
dek: Hawai’i was a kingdom with a queen, treaties and a seat among nations. In 1893, 13 businessmen backed by U.S. troops took it in a day. She fought back with paper, and lost. The deals they started run to a $2.3 billion buyout in 2026 and an Army lease on the kingdom’s old land that comes due in 2029.
summary: How missionary families, sugar money and a U.S. minister with troops took the Kingdom of Hawaii in 1893, and how Queen Liliʻuokalani fought back on paper.

blocks.text: Queen Liliʻuokalani. On January 17, 1893, she yielded “to the superior force of the United States of America.”

blocks.text: Sources: Blount Report (1893); 1897 anti-annexation petitions; Army ceded-land leases. See The Receipts.
2029 · A deadline on the Big Island
On August 16, 2029, a lease runs out on about 23,000 acres of the Big Island. The tenant is the U.S. Army. The rent for all 65 years: $1. The land once belonged to the Kingdom of Hawaii.
Most of us learned a softer story. Missionaries brought the Bible. Business brought the trouble. Washington just watched, and the islands drifted into becoming the 50th state.
That story skips the paperwork.
Hawaii wasn’t taken by an invading army. It was acquired, one signed document at a time.

Follow the lease backward, and the documents line up. In 2026, investors bought out Alexander & Baldwin, a company founded by two missionaries’ sons who were brothers-in-law. In 1898, Congress took the islands with a vote that skipped the treaty process. In 1893, a U.S. diplomat wrote a letter that put a price on a deposed queen. That same year, a militia commander listed the rifles that came from a Honolulu store. Weeks before the coup, the Navy secretary had said Washington would be “very glad to annex Hawaii.”
Hawaii wasn’t taken by an invading army. It was acquired, one signed document at a time. A small circle of island families drew up the papers. Washington’s man in Honolulu brought the troops.
The first document came from a church office in Boston.
1810–1863 · Boston told its missionaries to stay, just as the kingdom’s land went on sale.

The mission began as a New England project. In 1810 a group of ministers and businessmen founded the American Board of Commissioners for Foreign Missions. Its first missionaries landed in Hawaii in 1820. A Boston trader named James Hunnewell sailed with them. His firm later became C. Brewer & Co., one of the islands’ big sugar agencies, by one account.
For a generation, Boston paid and the missionaries preached. Then, in 1848 and 1849, the board rewrote the deal.

blocks.title: Meanwhile, in Sunday school: The kids who owned the mission fleet

blocks.text: From 1856 to 1905, about 150,000 American children bought ten-cent shares to pay for a series of mission ships, every one named Morning Star. Sunday-school kids across the mainland became small investors in the Pacific missions.
Images of Old Hawaiʻi; Australian National Maritime Museum

The board’s ruling committee decided that “new and additional motives must be presented” to keep its married missionaries in the islands. Its plan, as a later appeal for the missionaries’ school put it, was to turn “the missionaries into citizens and pastors.”
In 1848 the king divided the kingdom’s land in a reform called the Great Māhele. For the first time, land could be private property. A law in 1850 let foreigners buy it.

Ordinary Hawaiians got very little. James H. Blount, a former congressman sent to investigate in 1893, found the common people left “with an insignificant interest in lands—27,830 acres.” That is under 1% of the kingdom’s roughly 4 million acres. Most of the rest went to the chiefs, the crown and the government.

Missionaries sat near the controls. A former missionary doctor, Gerrit P. Judd, was the kingdom’s finance minister from 1846 to 1853. In August 1850, the king’s top advisers, his Privy Council, let missionaries with eight or more years of service buy up to 560 acres each at a discount. That comes from accounts that quote the council’s minutes.

The mission’s supply store changed hands too. Samuel N. Castle ran it. In 1851, when Boston cut support, he and Amos Starr Cooke, a mission teacher, signed partnership papers, according to the company’s own history. Their firm became Castle & Cooke.
The record doesn’t show the board picking anyone’s land. It changed their job, and the land was there to buy.
1864–1891 · A missionary’s son-in-law helped negotiate the treaty that made sugar rich.
The next generation built its firms the way royal houses built alliances: at the altar.

King Kalākaua (center) with members of the Reciprocity Commission, including John Owen Dominis and U.S. Commissioner Henry A. Peirce, 1874. The treaty they pushed for let Hawaiian sugar into America duty-free. Public domain

Amos Cooke had daughters. On January 26, 1864, Martha Cooke married Samuel T. Alexander, a missionary’s son who managed sugar plantations. On June 29, 1865, Juliette Cooke married Joseph B. Atherton, a clerk at Castle & Cooke. That same year, Atherton became a junior partner. Alexander’s sister Emily married Henry P. Baldwin, another missionary’s son. Alexander and Baldwin went into sugar together. Their company, Alexander & Baldwin, was a firm of brothers-in-law.
Cooke’s son Charles M. Cooke later became president of C. Brewer, which sold the plantations’ sugar.

The most valuable wedding was Sybil Judd’s. The former missionary’s daughter married Henry A.P. Carter, a part owner of C. Brewer. Carter then helped negotiate the 1875 Reciprocity Treaty with the United States. It let Hawaiian sugar into America duty-free.

Signers of the Jan. 16, 1893 request for U.S. troops. None was Native Hawaiian. Citizenship records show seven were not Hawaiian subjects; Blount’s 1893 count said six. Pink: missionaries’ sons and grandsons (3).

Sources: Blount Report (1893), pp. 583–588; Kam and Lyons, Hawaiian Journal of History 53 (2019).

The treaty worked like a winning lottery ticket that paid every year. Hawaiian sugar shipped to the United States rose from under 20 million pounds a year to about 200 million by 1887, by one economist’s count. Claus Spreckels, a San Francisco sugar refiner, later put the yearly windfall “in the neighborhood of $5,000,000.” From 1883 to 1891 Carter represented the kingdom in Washington as its minister, the top diplomat.
The marriages built the firms. A son-in-law built the market. Then the money went looking for power.
1878–1887 · The Sugar King got a cabinet replaced. A rival club rewrote the king’s job at gunpoint.
Spreckels went first, according to W.D. Alexander, the kingdom’s surveyor-general.

On the night of July 1, 1878, Spreckels met King Kalākaua. The king then asked his whole cabinet to resign. The new cabinet gave Spreckels the right to Maui stream water for 30 years at $500 a year. Alexander was a missionary’s son and a political enemy of the king, so his telling is one-sided. But the water grant is on the record.
By 1886 the government owed him hundreds of thousands of dollars, by Alexander’s count. Kalākaua paid him off with a loan from London. The Sugar King lost his grip on the palace.

Then a rival group made its move. In 1887 a secret society of white residents, the Hawaiian League, about 405 strong, backed by an armed militia, forced Kalākaua to sign a new constitution. Hawaiians called it the Bayonet Constitution. Lorrin A. Thurston, a lawyer and a grandson of missionaries, helped write it. Missionary sons led the league, historians say.

The new rules shrank the king’s power. To vote for the upper house, a man now needed $3,000 in property or $600 a year in income. Asian residents lost the vote. Foreign residents of American or European descent could vote without becoming citizens.

That same year, the United States renewed the sugar treaty with a new condition. Hawaii had to give the U.S. the exclusive right to enter Pearl Harbor and keep a naval coaling and repair station there.
Jan. 14–17, 1893 · The guns came from the store. The money men took the treasury.

Six years later, the king’s sister, now queen, wanted royal power back. On January 14, 1893, Queen Liliʻuokalani moved to replace the 1887 constitution. That afternoon, a 13-man Committee of Safety formed to stop her.

Blount counted the 13: “Six are Hawaiian subjects; five are American citizens; one English, and one German.” Three were island-born sons and grandsons of missionaries: Thurston; William O. Smith, a lawyer; and William R. Castle, a lawyer and Samuel Castle’s son. Not one of the 13 was Native Hawaiian.

Every takeover needs a vendor. After the coup, Col. John H. Soper, the new government’s military commander, listed where his weapons came from. The biggest batch of store-bought guns came from Castle & Cooke: about 18 Winchester repeating rifles and 24 revolvers. E.O. Hall & Son, a Honolulu hardware firm, supplied 14 more guns and all 16,100 cartridges. The guns, Soper told Blount, were “part of the stock in the store.”

“Part of the stock in the store.” About 18 Winchester rifles and 24 revolvers came from Castle & Cooke, by the militia commander’s list. No record shows any company board voting to back the coup. Illustration

On January 17 the committee read a proclamation ending the monarchy. Twelve of the 13 took seats on its councils or in its offices. Sanford B. Dole, a judge and a missionary’s son, became president. The money posts went to the money men. Peter C. Jones, who by most accounts ran C. Brewer, became finance minister. Samuel M. Damon, a partner in Bishop & Co., Hawaii’s leading bank, became vice president.
The circle closed later in the decade. Jones co-founded the Bank of Hawaii with Charles M. Cooke and J.B. Atherton, the mission teacher’s son and son-in-law.

The sugar world was split, and that matters. Spreckels, still the biggest grower, sided with the queen, by most accounts. Theo H. Davies, who owned another big sugar firm, opposed annexation. No record shows any company board voting to back the coup. The store’s stock showed up anyway.
The stores armed the committee. Washington’s man gave it cover.
1892–1893 · Washington said it would be “very glad” to annex Hawaii, 17 days before U.S. troops landed.

The U.S. minister in Honolulu, John L. Stevens, wanted Hawaii for America. He put it in writing. In early 1892 he asked his boss, Secretary of State James G. Blaine, how far the minister and naval commander “may deviate from established, international rules and precedents” in a revolution. He was picturing a Native Hawaiian uprising, and no reply is on record. Later that year he urged Blaine’s successor, John W. Foster, to take “bold and vigorous measures for annexation.”

On December 30, 1892, the Navy secretary, Benjamin Tracy, briefed Rear Adm. Joseph S. Skerrett, who was about to take command in the Pacific. “The wishes of the Government have changed,” Tracy said, as Skerrett later testified. “They will be very glad to annex Hawaii.” Tracy added that “none but the ordinary legal means” could be used. He also said, “I have no instructions to give you.”
Seventeen days later, U.S. troops were ashore.

On January 16, 1893, the committee wrote to Stevens: “We are unable to protect ourselves without aid.” Around 5 p.m., sailors and marines from the USS Boston came ashore. Stevens said they were there to protect American lives and property. But the officers housed them near the government building, in full view of the palace, Blount found.

The next day the proclamation was read. Stevens recognized the new government before the queen’s police station and barracks had surrendered. U.S. troops fired no shots. They didn’t need to. The queen yielded, she wrote, “to the superior force of the United States of America.”

No written order from Washington has ever turned up. President Benjamin Harrison told the Senate the coup “was not in any way promoted by this Government.” But his Navy had said yes to the goal, and his minister had landed the troops.
Sailors and marines from the USS Boston in Honolulu, January 1893. They fired no shots. The U.S. minister recognized the new government before the queen’s police station and barracks had surrendered.
The paper trail stops at Stevens’s desk. The troops didn’t.
1893–1898 · The “ripe pear” letter came after the coup, with $70,000 for the queen.
Behind the politics sat a sugar problem. The U.S. McKinley Tariff of 1890 let all foreign sugar in duty-free and paid American growers a bounty, a cash bonus per pound. Hawaii’s advantage was gone.
“The Hawaiian pear is now fully ripe.” Stevens wrote it on February 1, 1893, two weeks after the coup. The same letter priced the deposed queen at $70,000. Illustration
Everyone quotes one line from Stevens. “The Hawaiian pear is now fully ripe,” he wrote, “and this is the golden hour for the United States to pluck it.”
It is February 1, 1893, two weeks after the coup. It wasn’t a signal before the takeover. It was the pitch to close it.

Read the rest, and it looks like a buyout offer. Stevens proposed that the United States pay Hawaii’s planters a sugar bounty of “6 mills per pound.” A mill is a tenth of a cent. He priced the royal family too. The deposed queen would get $70,000. So would her 17-year-old heir, Princess Kaʻiulani.

Thurston and Castle went to Washington to negotiate an annexation treaty. President Harrison sent it to the Senate on February 15. Then a new president tore it up. Grover Cleveland withdrew the treaty in March. In December 1893 he told Congress the overthrow was “an act of war,” carried out with the help of an American diplomat.

That same month, the mission’s old head office weighed in. The board’s magazine, the Missionary Herald, wrote: “Never was there a revolution more warranted by facts.” Putting the queen back, it said, would be “a gross outrage.” The board that turned its preachers into settlers in 1849 cheered the coup in 1893.

The new government waited Cleveland out. In 1897 Native Hawaiians signed petitions against annexation. One petition alone carried 21,269 names. A new treaty got only 46 Senate votes, short of the 60 it needed.

So Congress took a shortcut. In 1898, during the war with Spain, it passed the Newlands Resolution, which needed only a simple majority in each house. President William McKinley signed it on July 7. The planters never got Stevens’s bounty; an 1894 tariff had already restored their advantage. But the islands changed hands.

“...earnestly protest against the annexation of the said Hawaiian Islands to the said United States of America in any form or shape.” Women of Hilo signing for the Women’s Hawaiian Patriotic League, 1897. Congress annexed Hawaiʻi anyway, by simple majority.
1898–1940 · Annexation handed the islands to five firms.
After 1898 Hawaii was a U.S. territory, ruled by Washington-appointed governors.
By 1920 the Big Five controlled about 94% of the sugar crop, by one count. Illustration

They were called the Big Five: Castle & Cooke, Alexander & Baldwin, C. Brewer, American Factors and Theo H. Davies. By 1920 they controlled about 94% of the sugar crop, by one count. In 1940 a federal labor investigator, E.J. Eagen, told a committee of Congress that they controlled “thirty-seven of the forty plantations.” “There are no independent banks,” he reported. Their shipping line, Matson, had “a virtual strangle hold on the Islands.”

Three of the five sat in this story from the start. Castle & Cooke was Matson’s shipping agent from 1907 to 1963. Alexander & Baldwin bought into Matson in 1908 and later owned it outright. C. Brewer’s president had held the purse in the coup government.

The rules bent their way. In 1921 Congress passed the Hawaiian Homes Commission Act to put Native Hawaiians back on the land. The law left out “all cultivated sugar-cane lands.” Prince Jonah Kūhiō Kalanianaʻole, Hawaii’s delegate in Congress, agreed with the sugar interests to leave the cane land out. The same law also deleted an old rule that no corporation could hold more than 1,000 acres.

The grandsons got the top jobs. George R. Carter and Lawrence M. Judd, both missionary grandsons, served as territorial governors. William R. Castle Jr., a grandson of the mission storekeeper, became Under Secretary of State, the department’s number-two job, from 1931 to 1933.

blocks.title: The model traveled: From a Hilo school to Carlisle

blocks.text: Samuel Chapman Armstrong grew up in the mission world. His father, a missionary, became the kingdom’s minister of public instruction. In 1868 Armstrong founded Hampton Institute in Virginia, modeled on the Hilo mission’s manual-labor school. Booker T. Washington trained there.

In 1879 Armstrong wrote to Army officer Richard Henry Pratt about Pratt’s plan for the Carlisle Indian School. Pratt dropped Hampton’s practice of sending students home. The goal, he said in 1883, was to “immerse the Indians in our civilization ... until they are thoroughly soaked.”
Beyer, History of Education Quarterly (2007); Carlisle Indian School Digital Resource Center
The historian Lawrence Fuchs later judged that no mainland community of similar size had been run so completely by so few people for so long.
1894–2029 · The coup ended in 1893. The lease ends in 2029.

In 1894 and 1895, the new Republic of Hawaii folded the crown lands, the monarchy’s own estates, into public land. In 1898 about 1.8 million acres of crown and government land passed to the United States. In 1959 most of it went to the new State of Hawaii. Today these are called the “ceded lands.”

blocks.title: Sidebar: The missionaries’ store became Dole

blocks.text: A Honolulu mission shop from 1851 grew into Dole, and only changed its name.

items: 1851: A mission storekeeper and a mission teacher found Castle & Cooke in Honolulu. Dole’s SEC filing says it “was founded in Hawaii in 1851.”
1893: About 18 rifles and 24 revolvers used by the coup’s forces came from Castle & Cooke’s store stock, per the militia commander’s list.
Wrong Dole: Sanford Dole led the 1893 government. His cousin James, the pineapple man, arrived in 1899.
1932: Castle & Cooke takes control of James Dole’s Depression-crushed pineapple company. TIME reports Dole is out as general manager.
1964–68: Castle & Cooke buys Standard Fruit, a New Orleans banana firm whose founders ran the Honduran town of La Ceiba. Their bank printed its own money.
1972: Honduran bananas get a Dole sticker. In 1991 Castle & Cooke becomes Dole Food Company. Same corporation, new name.

One poison, two rulebooks: The U.S. pulled most uses of DBCP, a pesticide that made men sterile, in 1977. Hawaii pineapple got a pass until 1985. When Dow halted shipments, Standard Fruit called it “a breach of contract.”
Jobs: In the 1970s, Dole’s Hawaii pineapple jobs fell from 11,569 to 5,700 as growing moved to cheaper countries.

blocks.text: The accusations: Over the decades, Standard Fruit and Dole have faced accusations abroad. None was proven, and Dole has denied them.
The coup stayed in 1893. The company kept going.
Sources and ratings: “Hawaii – Dole Sidebar Sources” (SIDE EYE research file).

Five years later, the state rented about 29,300 acres of ceded land to the U.S. Army for 65 years. The rent was $1 per lease. The biggest lease, at Pōhakuloa on the Big Island, runs out on August 16, 2029.
$1 per lease, for 65 years. The Army’s biggest lease on the kingdom’s old land, at Pōhakuloa, runs out on August 16, 2029. Illustration

In May 2025 the state land board rejected the Army’s environmental study for Pōhakuloa, a required step toward a new lease. If the leases end, the land goes back to the state. It does not go back to the Hawaiian people or to a kingdom. But for the first time in 65 years, someone can set new terms on the kingdom’s old land.
The families, meanwhile, cashed out. In 2013, the Castle family’s ranch and foundation sold most of Kailua town on Oʻahu to Alexander & Baldwin for $373 million.

The companies went to strangers. Alexander & Baldwin sold its 41,000 acres of Maui sugar land in 2018. On March 12, 2026, Alexander & Baldwin itself was taken private in a deal worth about $2.3 billion, including debt.
The families sold. The Army stayed. The clock runs out in 2029.
1909–1993 · One of the men who took her throne ended up minding her trust. Another’s grandson owned the morning paper.
William O. Smith was one of the 13 who ended Liliʻuokalani’s reign. In 1909 he became a trustee of her own trust, which she set up that year.

Thurston’s grandson, Thurston Twigg-Smith, took control of Honolulu’s morning newspaper, the Honolulu Advertiser, in 1961. The Justice Department cleared its sale to the Gannett chain on January 27, 1993, ten days after the overthrow’s 100th anniversary. Nothing shows the timing was planned.

So the soft story gets it backward. The missionaries’ families didn’t make way for business. Some of them became the business. Washington didn’t just watch. Its Navy said yes and its minister landed the troops.

blocks.title: What we can prove / what we can’t

blocks.text: Proven:

items: In 1848–49 the Boston board set out to make its missionaries “citizens and pastors.”
A new cabinet gave Spreckels 30 years of Maui water for $500 a year in 1878. The account of the cabinet’s firing comes from a political enemy of the king.
The 1887 constitution set money tests for voters and shut out Asians; the 1887 treaty renewal gave the U.S. rights at Pearl Harbor.
None of the 13 committee members was Native Hawaiian. Three were missionary sons or grandsons.
Navy Secretary Tracy said Washington would be “very glad to annex Hawaii” on December 30, 1892, adding that only legal means could be used (Skerrett’s testimony).
U.S. troops landed at the committee’s written request, and Stevens recognized the new government before the barracks surrendered.
Stevens’s February 1, 1893 letter proposed a planter bounty and $70,000 each for the queen and Kaʻiulani.
The 1921 homes law excluded cultivated sugar-cane land and dropped the corporate 1,000-acre limit.
W.O. Smith, one of the 13, became a trustee of the queen’s trust in 1909.
The state leases about 29,300 acres of ceded land to the Army at $1 per lease; Pōhakuloa’s lease ends August 16, 2029.

blocks.text: Likely:

items: Hunnewell’s firm became C. Brewer.
The 1850 land discount for long-serving missionaries (seen only as quoted).
Castle & Cooke grew out of the mission store (the company’s own history).
The 1940 Eagen report’s claims of Big Five control (an investigator’s claims in a heated hearing).

blocks.text: Not proven:

items: That Washington ordered or approved the overthrow in advance.
That any company voted for, paid for or donated weapons to the coup.
That the families planned 1849 through 1898 as one operation.
That sugar, rather than the queen’s new constitution, set off the coup itself.

blocks.text: The other side

Defenders of the overthrow’s leaders make a real case. Hawaii’s own politics set the timing. The 1892 legislature threw out four cabinets and passed lottery and opium bills. The queen moved to rewrite the constitution on her own. The committee’s leaders said they were defending a constitution, not a sugar price. U.S. troops had landed in Honolulu before, in 1874 and 1889, without toppling anyone.

The family web has an innocent reading too. Honolulu’s foreign elite was a few dozen families far from home, and small towns marry their neighbors. The missionaries also brought real gifts: a written Hawaiian alphabet, schools and a reading public.

Weigh it honestly. The timing argument is fair. But the 1887 voting rules were what kept the missionary sons and merchants in power, so “political, not economic” is a false choice. The earlier landings came at the Hawaiian government’s request or went to guard the U.S. legation, the American diplomatic office. In 1893 the request came from the rebels.
Why the gap?
One reading says this was a small world doing what small worlds do. A few dozen families married each other, ran businesses and grabbed each opening as it came.
The other reading says a class knew what it wanted and used every opening on purpose, from the 1849 resolution to the 1887 constitution to the 1893 landing.
Either way, one fact stands. Thirteen men ended a Native Hawaiian kingdom, and not one of them was Native Hawaiian.

blocks.title: SIDE EYE · Sidebar: The SIDE EYE guide to overthrowing a kingdom (without firing a shot)

blocks.text: A how-to built entirely from the 1893 record.

items: Form a committee. Thirteen men will do. Call it the Committee of Safety. Not one of them needs to be Native Hawaiian. In 1893, not one was.
Shop local. E.O. Hall & Son, a Honolulu hardware firm, can supply all 16,100 cartridges.
Ask nicely. Write to the U.S. minister: “We are unable to protect ourselves without aid.” Sailors and marines come ashore around 5 p.m.
Skip the formalities. The U.S. minister recognizes your government before the queen’s barracks surrender. No shots required.
Divide the jobs. Twelve of the 13 get posts. Finance goes to Peter C. Jones, who by most accounts ran C. Brewer.
Name a price. Two weeks later, Stevens proposes $70,000 for the deposed queen. Her 17-year-old heir gets the same.
Land on your feet. In 1909, William O. Smith, one of the 13, becomes a trustee of the queen’s own trust.

blocks.text: Final step: have the President tell the Senate it “was not in any way promoted by this Government.” No written order has ever turned up.

The Files · Sidebar: What would sovereignty mean?

The 1993 apology admits Native Hawaiians never gave up their claim to sovereignty. It doesn’t say what sovereignty should look like, and Hawaiians themselves disagree. Here is the range of answers, from least Hawaiian self-government to most. Each has serious supporters and serious critics.

rows: Hawaiʻi stays a state. Programs limited by Hawaiian ancestry, like school admissions and homesteads, are opened to everyone or ended.
Today’s setup, kept or strengthened. State agencies serve Native Hawaiians inside the state system, with no separate Hawaiian government.
A Native Hawaiian government, recognized by the U.S., runs its own affairs, members and lands, much as federally recognized tribes do.
Hawaiʻi becomes its own country but signs a long-term compact: the U.S. provides defense and aid, and gets military access.
Hawaiʻi leaves the U.S. entirely, as a new nation or as the Hawaiian Kingdom, which some argue legally never ended.
The State of Hawaiʻi and the U.S., like any other state.
The State of Hawaiʻi. OHA trustees are elected by all voters.
A Native Hawaiian government elected by its members, alongside the state and federal governments. Congress keeps final say.
An independent Hawaiian government. Under the “occupation” theory, the kingdom’s own government, restored.
Ceded lands stay state trust land. The Home Lands ancestry rule is struck down or repealed.
The state holds ceded lands in trust and shares revenue with OHA. About 200,000 acres of Home Lands go to homesteaders at least 50% Hawaiian.
Some ceded lands and Home Lands could be transferred to it by negotiation.
The Hawaiian government controls the land. The compact sets terms for U.S. bases.
All 1.8 million acres of former crown and government lands return to Hawaiian control.
U.S. citizens, with no separate Native Hawaiian legal status.
U.S. citizens. Hawaiian ancestry qualifies people for certain programs.
Native Hawaiians enroll as members and stay U.S. citizens.
Hawaiian citizenship, rules to be decided. Compact citizens today can live and work in the U.S. without visas.
A Hawaiian nationality. Debated: descendants of kingdom subjects, long-time residents, or everyone.
U.S. bases stay. The state decides on the Army’s land leases when they expire in 2029.
No change. The U.S. handles defense.
The U.S. handles defense and can keep other countries’ forces out (“strategic denial”).
U.S. bases leave or stay by treaty. Hawaiʻi hosts the U.S. Indo-Pacific Command.
Rice v. Cayetano (2000): the Supreme Court ruled 7–2 that Hawaiian-only voting for OHA was unconstitutional.
Hawaiʻi now: OHA (1978), Hawaiian Home Lands (1921), the Mauna Kea authority (2022).
Federally recognized tribes. A 2016 rule opened this path; nobody has used it. The Akaka Bill stalled in the Senate in 2006.
The Marshall Islands, Micronesia (1986) and Palau (1994), all UN members. Compacts renewed in 2024: $7.1 billion over 20 years.
The kingdom itself, which had treaties with the U.S., Britain and France. No annexation treaty was ratified. A 2001 tribunal declined to rule without the U.S.
The challengers in today’s lawsuits: Students for Fair Admissions and the Pacific Legal Foundation.
The State of Hawaiʻi, which is defending the ancestry rules in court and raised funding in 2022.
Akaka Bill supporters. Ka Lāhui Hawaiʻi (founded 1987) sought recognition while keeping UN decolonization on the table.
No major Hawaiian group makes it a first choice. It is one of three options the UN recognized in 1960.
The Nation of Hawaiʻi (Dennis “Bumpy” Kanahele). The Hawaiian Kingdom movement (David Keanu Sai).
Treats an Indigenous people as just a race, and breaks promises Congress made in 1921 and 1959.
It isn’t self-government. Lawmakers can cut it, courts can strike it, and 29,000+ people still wait for homesteads.
Critics on the right call it race-based government. Many sovereignty activists say it shrinks a nation into a tribe.
Built for small Pacific nations that rely on U.S. aid. Untested for 1.4 million people woven into America.
No government or court recognizes it, and it would upend the lives of 1.4 million U.S. citizens.

blocks.text: What’s already happened:

rows: A federal rule created a path to tribe-style recognition. No Native Hawaiian government has used it.
The state raised OHA’s yearly land-trust payment to $21.5 million, gave Hawaiian Home Lands $600 million, and created a Mauna Kea authority that takes over by 2028.
Hawaiian Home Lands awarded about 2,600 homestead leases, up from 84 the year before. More than 29,000 people are still waiting.

blocks.text: Ask yourself:

items: 1. In 1959, 94% of voters said yes to statehood, but independence wasn’t on the ballot. Does that vote settle the question?
2. Is a program for Native Hawaiians a racial preference or a promise to an Indigenous people? Can it be both?
3. Who should get a vote on Hawaiʻi’s future: Native Hawaiians, everyone who lives there, or all Americans?
